title: Steel from ore without fossil carbon at competitive global scale

concept.text: The innovation is a reliable, economically competitive industrial route that converts iron ore into usable steel without relying on fossil carbon for ore reduction, while achieving very low greenhouse-gas emissions across the full production chain. It encompasses ironmaking, conversion into specification-grade steel and finishing. The target is sustained commercial performance at a scale and cost that would allow broad deployment.

Hydrogen reduction and direct ore electrolysis are alternative approaches to this target. Hydrogen reduction uses hydrogen to remove oxygen from iron ore, producing iron that can subsequently be melted and refined. An electrolysis route would use electrical energy to drive reduction. Neither approach is required by the concept: the decisive advance would be an integrated process that meets the material-quality, reliability, emissions and economic goals.

Conceptual clarification: eliminating fossil carbon as the ore-reduction input does not require every steel product to contain no carbon. Steel composition and the origins of process inputs are separate questions. The proposed capability must account for any carbon-bearing additions, electrodes and other consumables within its emissions boundary, alongside electricity, reductants and finishing.

significance.text: A widely deployable process meeting this target could transform primary steel production while preserving steel’s established applications. Its direct consequence would be a substantially lower-emission way to make new iron and steel from ore. HYBRIT’s documented approach illustrates the mechanism by replacing coal and coke used in iron production with fossil-free hydrogen and electricity; its project announcement also reports steel use in vehicles, machinery, buildings and consumer products.

The revolutionary significance is conditional on cost, deployment and emissions performance being achieved together. An attractive pilot process would have limited industrial impact if commercial plants could not obtain sufficient clean energy, operate reliably or compete in their intended markets. Likewise, avoiding fossil reductants at the ironmaking stage would not by itself establish near-zero emissions for finished steel: upstream inputs, electricity generation, consumables and subsequent processing remain consequential.

Conditional synthesis: successful deployment could lower the emissions embodied in steel-intensive infrastructure and manufactured goods without requiring those applications to abandon steel. It would complement improvements in recycling and material efficiency. It would not, by itself, establish better fatigue life, corrosion resistance or other service properties, and competitive production costs would not automatically guarantee rapid replacement of existing industrial capacity.

missing_breakthrough.text: The target breakthrough is the combination of integrated ore-to-steel production, durable equipment, commercial throughput, competitive economics and very low full life-cycle emissions. The supplied evidence documents a substantial pilot program and its industrialization goal, but does not establish whether this complete capability remains unmet worldwide as of 1 November 2026. The challenge should therefore be understood as the capability being sought, without treating the available record as proof of its global absence.

Reduction chemistry and thermal management are concrete engineering considerations. The reviewed HYBRIT brochure explains that hydrogen reduction differs from natural-gas reduction in its chemistry and thermodynamics. Industrial integration must accommodate the resulting iron product through melting and steelmaking. These observations support the technical importance of process control and integration, but the supplied evidence does not establish that every such issue remains unresolved.

Engineering synthesis: convincing commercial performance would also require dependable energy and reductant supplies, acceptable reactor and electrode consumption, suitable raw materials and effective integration with finishing. Ore variability could affect process behavior, impurity management, yield and cost; equipment wear could affect maintenance intervals and availability. These are specific matters to investigate for each route, rather than a source-established list of outstanding failures. Hydrogen reduction and electrolysis may encounter different constraints, so evidence for one route cannot settle the readiness of the other.

current_state.text: On 27 August 2024, HYBRIT reported that its Luleå pilot plant had produced more than 5,000 tonnes of hydrogen-reduced iron and that the project had developed practices for melting sponge iron into crude steel. These are dated project-reported achievements. They establish substantial pilot progress but do not independently demonstrate sustained, economically competitive ore-to-finished-steel production at global scale.

The accompanying August 2024 HYBRIT brochure reports pilot-scale melting validation using Swerim’s 10-tonne electric arc furnace in Luleå. This furnace capacity describes the melting demonstration and should not be confused with the cumulative iron-production total. The brochure limits its headline emissions estimate to Scope 1 and Scope 2; that boundary does not establish near-zero full life-cycle emissions. Its industrialization plans describe intended next steps rather than demonstrated commercial operation.

The supplied review had a complete retained extraction of the HYBRIT announcement, but only a partial text extraction of the brochure: some PDF pages lacked extractable text, and its figures were not inspected. The production, furnace-capacity and emissions-boundary statements above were explicitly supported by the reviewed text. The incomplete extraction limits broader interpretation of the brochure and does not negate those documented statements.

The earlier research attributes a March 2025 commissioning milestone to Boston Metal: a multi-anode molten-oxide-electrolysis steel cell reportedly produced tonnage of metal. However, the supplied review had no retained text for the cited announcement, so its contents, date and milestone details could not be verified. This remains a reported lead in the research record. Even if confirmed, a commissioning run would not alone demonstrate sustained competitive production through finished steel.

The earlier research also attributes a 23 February 2026 report to Maria Gallucci and describes an equipment failure at Boston Metal’s Brazilian critical-metals facility. The supplied review had no retained text for that article, leaving the date, failure details and facility attribution unverified. Accordingly, this citation cannot establish that the steel cell failed, or that the incident was confined to a separate facility. Missing evidence does not show that the reported incident was false.

Evidence limitation: the supplied record contains no freshness assessment establishing worldwide status as of 1 November 2026. It therefore supports the dated HYBRIT achievements and identifies further reports needing verification, but cannot establish the latest global commercial position. This limitation does not invalidate the historical pilot results or resolve whether the overall target has since been achieved elsewhere.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: independently audited, sustained operation across multiple commercial plants would convert a declared range of representative ores into several specification-grade steel products. The demonstrations would cover the integrated production chain through finishing, with disclosed throughput, yields, product quality and operating conditions. Multiple plants and independent audits are proposed ways to test transferability and credibility; they are not standards established by the supplied sources.
completion_criteria.label: Multiple audited plants sustain ore conversion into finished specification-grade steel

completion_criteria.text: Proposed economic and reliability evidence: plant data would establish equipment life, electrode and other consumable use, maintenance needs, availability and performance during routine operating variation. Cost accounts would include energy, reductants, raw materials, consumables, maintenance, capital costs and finishing, with transparent assumptions for comparison against conventional production in the intended markets. A commissioning run alone would leave sustained performance and commercial economics unresolved.
completion_criteria.label: Plant data establish sustained reliability and full production costs

completion_criteria.text: Proposed environmental evidence: independently examined life-cycle accounts would include electricity supply, reductant production, electrodes, upstream material inputs, ironmaking, steelmaking and finishing under a clearly declared boundary. The assessment would distinguish direct and purchased-energy emissions from wider supply-chain emissions. This broader accounting is necessary to test the concept’s life-cycle ambition beyond the Scope 1 and Scope 2 boundary identified in HYBRIT’s reviewed brochure.
completion_criteria.label: Independently examined life-cycle accounts distinguish operational and supply-chain emissions

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundaries: an evaluation would specify in advance what counts as sustained operation, very low emissions and competitive cost, including the relevant production period, energy assumptions and market conditions. No numerical thresholds for these terms are established by the supplied record. Reproducibility across plants, ore sources and product grades would establish demonstrated breadth within the tested conditions; finite demonstrations would not prove suitability for every ore, steel grade, location or energy system.
completion_criteria.label: Predeclared performance criteria and reproducibility evidence establish demonstrated limits

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: MET-03, “Repeated, high-grade recycling of mixed steel scrap,” is the closest complement. MET-02 concerns primary production from ore; MET-03 concerns preserving or restoring quality through repeated scrap recycling. MET-10, “Repeated upcycling of mixed aluminum scrap into demanding alloys,” shares the challenge of controlling variable feedstocks and impurities, but concerns a different metal and a recycling route. None of these concepts substitutes for the others.

Roster-based synthesis: MET-01, “Predictive metallurgy from composition to lifetime,” could help connect processing choices and impurities to final steel performance, while MET-02 concerns the production route’s emissions, cost and industrial reliability. MET-05, “Titanium at mass-market structural-metal cost,” shares the ambition of making a structural metal economically accessible through production advances, but has a different material target and does not establish low-emission steelmaking.

Roster-based synthesis: MET-04, “Structural metals that repeatedly heal fatigue damage in service,” MET-09, “Uncoated structural alloys for very high temperatures in oxidizing environments,” and MET-11, “Structural alloys with broadly reliable intrinsic corrosion resistance,” concern behavior during service. A successful MET-02 process could supply material for demanding applications, but would not by itself confer self-healing, oxidation resistance or corrosion resistance.

Roster-based synthesis: MET-06, “A practical structural alloy system for sustained fusion-reactor conditions,” targets performance in a specialized service environment. MET-07, “Manufacturable, damage-tolerant bulk metallic glasses,” targets a distinct material structure and manufacturability challenge. MET-08, “Practical room-temperature superplastic forming of common alloys,” targets forming behavior. Their production or processing requirements could interact with energy use and industrial economics, but each remains distinct from competitive low-emission ore-to-steel production.

unresolved_issues: Worldwide achievement or non-achievement of the complete target as of 1 November 2026 remains unestablished because no freshness assessment was supplied.
Boston Metal’s cited commissioning date, cell configuration, production quantity and operating scope require retained source evidence.
The cited Canary Media report’s date, equipment-failure details and facility attribution remain unverified; its implications for steel-cell reliability cannot be resolved.
Some HYBRIT brochure pages lacked extractable text and its figures were not inspected in the supplied review, limiting assessment beyond the explicitly reviewed passages.
The record does not independently establish commercial cost competitiveness, sustained equipment reliability or near-zero full life-cycle emissions at major industrial scale.
Numerical thresholds for very low emissions, sustained operation, commercial scale and cost competitiveness remain to be defined, along with representative ore and product coverage.

brief.title: Affordable steel from ore without fossil fuels
possible: The steel in cars, buildings and machinery could come from ore processed without fossil carbon to remove its oxygen. Steelmakers could produce finished steel reliably, at competitive cost and on a scale suited to widespread use, with very low emissions across the whole production chain.
why: This would lower the emissions built into infrastructure and manufactured goods while preserving steel’s established uses. It would complement recycling and efforts to use materials more efficiently.

sources.who: HYBRIT, a collaboration between SSAB, LKAB and Vattenfall
sources.showed: HYBRIT reported producing iron with hydrogen, which removes oxygen from ore, and developing a process for melting that iron into crude steel. Customers were already using its steel in manufactured products.
sources.quote: So far, more than 5,000 tonnes of hydrogen-reduced iron have been produced at HYBRIT’s pilot plant in Luleå.
sources.cited_for: The pilot demonstrates progress from ore through ironmaking and steelmaking using hydrogen and electricity.
sources.not_established: Pilot results do not establish sustained commercial production, competitive full costs or very low emissions across the whole production chain.

sources.showed: This is an announcement about a commissioning run of a steelmaking cell that uses electricity to remove oxygen from ore.
sources.cited_for: It concerns an alternative route that uses electricity directly to turn ore into metal.
sources.not_established: A commissioning run alone would not establish sustained reliability, competitive costs or production through finished steel.

sources.showed: This is a report about an equipment failure at Boston Metal’s Brazilian critical-metals facility.
sources.cited_for: It raises a question about equipment reliability at Boston Metal.
sources.not_established: A failure at a critical-metals facility would not by itself establish the reliability of the steelmaking cell.

shown: HYBRIT reports that its pilot plant produced more than 5,000 tonnes of iron using hydrogen. It also developed a process for melting that iron into crude steel and reports customer use of its steel. These are results from one pilot programme; sustained commercial performance remains to be demonstrated.
missing: The target requires sustained production from ore through finished steel that meets product specifications across multiple commercial plants.
It requires equipment life, maintenance needs and full production costs that support reliable, competitive operation.
It requires very low emissions across energy supplies, materials, consumables and every production stage.

milestones.label: Multiple plants sustain production of finished steel
milestones.explanation: Independent audits would have to show sustained production from representative ores into finished steels meeting product specifications at multiple commercial plants. This would test whether the process transfers between plants.

milestones.label: Plant operation establishes reliability and competitive full costs
milestones.explanation: Plant data would have to establish equipment life, maintenance, consumable use and full production costs under routine operating variation. This would test whether dependable output can compete in its intended markets.

milestones.label: Independent accounts establish emissions across the production chain
milestones.explanation: Independent examination would have to count emissions from energy, materials and every production stage, separating plant emissions from supply-chain emissions. This would test the full environmental claim.

milestones.label: Agreed criteria and repeat results establish practical limits
milestones.explanation: Evaluations would have to set performance criteria in advance and reproduce results across plants, ores and steel grades. This would establish where the capability works under tested conditions.

uncertain: The thresholds for sustained operation, very low emissions, commercial scale and competitive cost still need defining.
Hydrogen and direct electrical routes may face different limits across ores, steel grades, locations and energy supplies.

page.title: Primary steelmaking without fossil reductants
page.definition: An industrial route converts iron ore into crude steel using hydrogen or electricity, rather than fossil carbon, to remove oxygen. It is commercially available at production-cost parity with conventional steelmaking and meets the IEA’s scrap-adjusted near-zero greenhouse-gas emissions limit, including specified upstream sources.

goal.need: The IEA’s 2022 benchmarks imply a more than sevenfold emissions gap between best-available coal-based ore-to-steel production and its near-zero limit. Its 2025 assessment estimates a 50–140% cost premium for early commercial plants using 100% hydrogen rather than the blast-furnace/basic-oxygen-furnace route, depending on region.

figures.caption: IEA 2022 emissions comparison with zero scrap input
columns: kg CO₂e per tonne of crude steel
rows: Coal blast furnace–basic oxygen furnace: best available technology
Natural-gas direct reduction–electric arc furnace: best available technology
figures.note: The conventional-route values are analytical benchmarks, not plant measurements. The emissions boundary ends at crude steel casting.

statements.quote: by replacing coal and coke in the production of iron with fossil-free hydrogen and electricity.
statements.context: The initiative identifies this substitution as its means of virtually eliminating steel-industry carbon dioxide emissions.

statements.quote: To catalyse the development and demonstration of cost competitive solutions for the efficient decarbonization of hard to abate energy intensive industries
statements.context: The mission covers steel, cement, chemicals and other energy-intensive industries.

statements.quote: Near-zero emission steel is the preferred choice in global markets
statements.context: Opening clause of the Steel Breakthrough Goal reproduced in the IEA’s assessment.

completion.title: A fossil-reductant-free primary steelmaking route operates commercially at cost parity and near-zero emissions.
completion.criterion: A complete ore-to-crude-steel route using no fossil carbon for ore reduction operates commercially at production-cost parity with conventional steelmaking in the same market. It meets the IEA limit of 400 − 350s kg CO₂e per tonne of crude steel, where s is scrap’s fraction of metallic inputs and s < 0.30 follows the IEA’s proposed primary-production cut-off. Use the IEA’s direct-plus-indirect emissions boundary through casting, including specified upstream sources. Commercial competitiveness corresponds to IEA TRL 10; production-cost parity follows Mission Innovation’s ambition.
completion.set_by: Atlas composite of the IEA’s emissions and technology-readiness criteria and Mission Innovation’s cost-parity ambition.
completion.basis: Searched IEA/G7 definitions, ResponsibleSteel progress levels, Steel Breakthrough goals and Mission Innovation targets. None supplies a joint fossil-reductant-free, globally competitive ore-to-finished-steel test. This narrower Atlas composite uses the published crude-steel boundary, emissions limits and commercial/parity criteria. It does not establish finished-product life-cycle emissions or deployment across global markets.

milestones.title: A laboratory prototype produces iron without fossil reductants (IEA TRL 4).
milestones.criterion: A laboratory prototype validates the ore-reduction process without fossil carbon, corresponding to technology readiness level 4. On 8 May 2013, Allanore, Yin and Sadoway reported iron extraction and oxygen evolution using chromium-alloy anodes in molten-oxide electrolysis, whose operating temperature exceeds 1,538 °C. This peer-reviewed result concerns an ironmaking component; it does not demonstrate a complete steelmaking plant.
milestones.set_by: International Energy Agency, technology-readiness convention applied in Iron and Steel Technology Roadmap, page 82.
milestones.threshold_quote: prototype developed in a laboratory environment

milestones.title: An ore-to-steel prototype works at scale in its intended operating conditions (IEA TRL 6).
milestones.criterion: A prototype works at scale under its intended deployment conditions, corresponding to IEA TRL 6. On 27 August 2024, HYBRIT reported over 5,000 tonnes of hydrogen-reduced iron and a process for melting it into crude steel. On 12 March 2025, Boston Metal reported commissioning a multi-inert-anode cell in Woburn, Massachusetts, describing tonnage output without specifying mass or run duration. These company announcements are not peer reviewed and do not establish formal TRL assignments.
milestones.set_by: International Energy Agency, technology-readiness convention applied in Iron and Steel Technology Roadmap, pages 82–83.
milestones.threshold_quote: testing in the conditions in which it will be deployed

milestones.title: A first commercial ore-to-steel plant demonstrates full-scale production (IEA TRL 8).
milestones.criterion: A first-of-a-kind commercial demonstration operates the complete ore-to-crude-steel route at full scale under its intended conditions, corresponding to IEA TRL 8. On 30 September 2026, Stegra reported that its Boden plant required additional capital for completion. On 2 June 2026, Boston Metal stated that it was focusing its efforts on critical metals. These company statements are not peer reviewed; neither reports achievement of this milestone.
milestones.set_by: International Energy Agency, technology-readiness convention applied in Iron and Steel Technology Roadmap, pages 82–83.

milestones.title: An ore-to-steel technology enters full commercial operation (IEA TRL 9).
milestones.criterion: The complete route is commercially available and operates in its relevant environment, corresponding to IEA TRL 9. SSAB’s 23 September 2025 release reports IEA/FMC-compliant steel combining HYBRIT iron with scrap at Montpelier, Iowa, where SSAB Zero is commercially available. It gives no scrap fraction or evidence of commercial-scale upstream ore reduction. This company report is not peer reviewed and does not establish this milestone for the complete primary route.
milestones.set_by: International Energy Agency, technology-readiness convention applied in Iron and Steel Technology Roadmap, page 82.

not_found: No published minimum annual output or operating duration was found for the combined completion capability.
No opened source establishes production-cost parity for an operating, complete fossil-reductant-free primary steelmaking route.
The Nature article’s full text could not be opened; its PubMed abstract supports the laboratory result reported here but gives no replicate count.

results.finding: HYBRIT’s pilot plant produced more than 5,000 tonnes of hydrogen-reduced iron.
results.detail: HYBRIT also reports an electric-arc-furnace process for melting the iron into crude steel and describes the value chain as semi-industrial. The announcement does not establish a formal TRL 6 assignment or show that the complete route operated under intended deployment conditions.
results.quote: So far, more than 5,000 tonnes of hydrogen-reduced iron have been produced at HYBRIT’s pilot plant in Luleå.

results.finding: HYBRIT’s hydrogen direct-reduction pilot produced more than 5,000 tonnes of sponge iron.
results.detail: Pilot trials validated the ore-to-steel process chain; HYBRIT’s sponge iron was also melted into crude steel in a pilot electric arc furnace. The report does not assign a formal TRL.
results.quote:
Sponge iron has been produced for extended 
periods under stable process conditions. More than 
5000 tonnes of fossil-free sponge iron have been 
produced so far.

results.finding: HYBRIT’s hydrogen direct-reduction pilot produced over 5,000 tonnes of sponge iron across pilot campaigns; some was used in melting trials.
results.detail: The pilot operated with hydrogen and tested melting in a 10-tonne electric arc furnace. The source reports testing in a relevant environment up to TRL 6/7; it does not establish an independently verified formal TRL assignment.
results.quote: When calculating different process point up to end of 2023, 175 has been evaluated during different campaigns in the pilot and more than 5000 ton of sponge iron has been produced. Some of the DRI and HBI have been further evaluated and used for melting trials in the pilot EAF.

results.finding: SIDERWIN: one 3 m iron ore electrolysis pilot was reported as validated at TRL 6.
results.detail: The source reports a pilot that produces iron plates and describes melting them into steel, but does not report that the pilot produced crude steel under intended deployment conditions.
results.quote: The project was led by ArcelorMittal together with 11 European partners and led to the development of a 3 m-long new experimental pilot which was validated at TRL 6.

results.finding: Luleå pilot produced its first hydrogen-reduced sponge iron in 2021; sample size not stated.
results.detail: The report describes a semi-industrial pilot, exceeding the laboratory scale required for m1. It is a company-authored report.
results.quote:
In the 
spring of 2021, the first fossil-free sponge iron was produced 
where iron ore was reduced with pure hydrogen as reduction 
agent.

results.finding: Pilot electric arc furnace trials produced more than 1,000 tonnes of steel.
results.detail: The report says the ore-to-steel value chain was tested at pilot scale. Its facilities had lower production capacity than full-scale plants; industrial implementation was still forthcoming.
results.quote: More than 1000 tonnes of steel have been produced

results.finding: HYBRIT pilot produced sponge iron using hydrogen as the only reduction gas since 2021; sample size not specified.
results.detail: The semi-industrial pilot validates fossil-carbon-free ore reduction, exceeding the laboratory-prototype stage.
results.quote: Since 2021 the direct reduction pilot plant has been operated using only hydrogen as reduction gas.

results.finding: HYBRIT sponge iron was melted in a 10-tonne pilot electric arc furnace; number of trials not specified.
results.detail: The source reports pilot-scale reduction and melting, rather than a complete commercial plant operating at full scale.
results.quote: The process has been verified on a pilot scale by melting HYBRITs sponge iron in Swerim´s 10-tonne electric arc furnace at SWERIM facility in Luleå.

results.finding: Volteron pilot: one electrolysis cell produces about 140 kg of metallic iron in four plates.
results.detail: The pilot demonstrates ore reduction by electrolysis without fossil carbon. It is an ironmaking component, not a complete steelmaking plant.
results.quote: 2025: Commissioning of a 1 m² Volteron pilot plant allowing the production of about 140 kg of metallic iron in a row of 4 plates, in a cell equipped of 2 cathodes / 3 anodes.

results.finding: Molten oxide electrolysis extracted iron and evolved oxygen using chromium-alloy anodes; sample size not stated; temperature exceeded 1,538 °C.
results.detail: The result concerns an ironmaking component, not a complete steelmaking plant.
results.quote: Here we show that anodes comprising chromium-based alloys exhibit limited consumption during iron extraction and oxygen evolution by MOE.

results.finding: ZESTY hydrogen direct reduction achieved 90% metallization in 18 pilot trials on one goethite/hematite ore.
results.detail: The electrically heated pilot reactor used hydrogen as the reductant and produced direct reduced iron. The result validates the ironmaking process, not a complete steelmaking plant.
results.quote: This paper focuses on 18 pilot plant trials at the ZESTY pilot plant using a single goethite/hematite ore, enabling a comparative analysis of various operating parameters of that specific ore. The highest level of metallization was found to be 90% for the investigated goethite/hematite ore

results.finding: CISRI’s pure-hydrogen shaft-furnace demonstration line: 1 line achieved 97.0–99.4% metallization.
results.detail: The paper reports separate melting tests on the reduced iron. The supplied text does not establish that an integrated ore-to-crude-steel prototype operated at scale under its intended deployment conditions.

results.finding: GISH hydrogen direct-reduction pilot: 4 campaigns produced iron at a final rate of more than 2 tons per week.
results.detail: The pilot demonstrated hydrogen reduction, and pilot-produced H-DRI was tested in a plant melting trial. The trial used a ladle metallurgy furnace as a proxy for an electric arc furnace; the report does not establish an ore-to-steel prototype operating under intended deployment conditions.
results.quote: The final output from the reactor was more than 2 tons per week.
